article_title: Rotoris bags Rs 70 Cr to expand its luxury watch business
article_excerpt:
Rotoris bags Rs 70 Cr to expand its luxury watch business
The Gurugram-based independent luxury watchmaker plans to use the funds for research and development, expanded production, and growing its Rotoris House, its appointment-based space for meeting clients, presence in India and overseas.
Gurugram-based independent luxury watchmaker Rotoris has raised Rs 70 crore (~$8.5 million) in a Series A funding round led by early-stage investment firm Blume Ventures.
9Unicorns and Centricity also participated, bringing in family-office investors including Diwakar Goel, BlackRock’s global head of data, former Coca-Cola Asia-Pacific group president Atul Singh and Adhiraj Burman of the Dabur family. Actor and television host Rannvijay Singha also invested.
The company plans to use the funds for research and development, expanded production, and growing its Rotoris House, its appointment-based space for meeting clients, presence in India and overseas.
The Gurugram-based watchmaker claims its first collection of 2,100 numbered timepieces sold out within days of its February 2026 launch. It asserted that nearly 1,00,000 people have since registered for access, while 40% of demand comes from outside India, including the US, Dubai, and Australia.
Blume Ventures sees an opportunity to build an Indian luxury brand with international ambitions. “We are backing their vision to make an Indian brand shine amongst global icons, and the timing has never been better,” said Karthik Reddy, co-founder and managing partner of Blume Ventures.
Rotoris produces limited-run analogue watches, releasing collections as named chapters with published production numbers. Its Manifesta collection features natural-stone dials, including lapis lazuli and imperial jade, making each dial distinct.
Astonia is a 42mm chronograph, a watch with a stopwatch function, made using steel, titanium and carbon and powered by a Swiss movement. Each timepiece is assembled and tested by hand at the company’s Gurugram Atelier, with movements sourced from Switzerland or Japan depending on the collection.
“The design creates the desire, but the engineering, assembly and attention to detail earn the trust,” co-founder Prerna Gupta said.
Co-founder Aakash Anand described a Rotoris watch as “a symbol of ambition, worn on the wrist”. He said the company plans to open Rotoris House in New York because many of its customers live there.
The expansion comes as Indian consumers increasingly trade up to higher-priced watches. Luxury and high-end watches accounted for 70% of sales in FY25, up from 48% in FY20. Younger buyers are showing greater interest in mechanical watches, distinctive designs and limited editions.
Trade policy could also reshape competition. The India-EFTA Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement, which took effect in October 2025, is expected to reduce import duties on qualifying watches from member countries, including Switzerland, over time. This could support greater access for international brands while raising competitive pressure on domestic manufacturers.
Other Indian watchmakers are pursuing international growth. In September, Bangalore Watch Company raised $1.4 million from its own customers, including family-office principals and high-net-worth individuals. Rotoris had previously raised $3 million in seed funding in December 2025.

company_description: Botsync has raised $11 million led by IvyCap Ventures to advance its AI-powered industrial automation platform, improve robotics capabilities and expand its presence in India and global markets.
article_title: Botsync raises $11M to expand industrial automation
article_excerpt:
Botsync raises $11M to expand industrial automation
Botsync has raised $11 million led by IvyCap Ventures to advance its AI-powered industrial automation platform, improve robotics capabilities and expand its presence in India and global markets.
Singapore-headquartered Botsync has raised $11 million in a round led by IvyCap Ventures, a homegrown venture capital firm.
Other participants include Capital 2B, a deeptech investor; Taiwan-based accelerator and venture investor AppWorks; South-East Asian early-stage investor Iterative; Singapore angel network AngelCentral; Genesis Alternative Ventures; and angel investor Nalin Advani.
The round follows a January 2026 Series A extension led by SGInnovate, taking total funding above $20 million.
Founded in 2019, Botsync builds autonomous mobile robots (AMRs), or driverless material movers, and software that coordinates factory and distribution-centre operations. Its SyncOS platform connects robots, robotic arms, conveyors, machines and enterprise software, managing tasks and traffic through one interface. Its MAG robots move loads of up to 1.5 tonnes.
“As India’s manufacturing ecosystem evolves, solutions combining robotics, AI, and intelligent automation will play a critical role in driving efficiency and scale. We believe Botsync is well positioned to address this growing opportunity and expand its footprint across global markets,” said Vikram Gupta, Founder and Managing Partner of IvyCap Ventures.
Funds will add SyncOS tools for throughput optimisation, predictive maintenance and operational analytics, helping factories move goods more efficiently, spot faults early and use operating data to improve performance. Botsync will also improve MAG reliability, add Indian engineering and project-delivery staff, deepen local automation partnerships, and expand in Australia and the US.
India is both a market and capability centre, with a Bengaluru office and experience centre serving automotive and fast-moving consumer goods manufacturers. Chief executive Rahul Nambiar said the opportunity lies in “connecting robots, machines and software systems” so facilities operate more efficiently.
Botsync claims more than 70 projects across six countries, over two million production tasks and 99% uptime. Its customers include Caterpillar, Ford, Nestlé, Honda, Coca-Cola and Kimberly-Clark. It says some customers recover their investment within 24 months through reduced forklift use and manual handling.
The raise comes as robotics investment in India gathers pace, although from a small base. Tracxn data put startup funding at $63.2 million across 15 rounds by July 2026, compared with $26.7 million across 24 rounds in the same period of 2025. Recent deals included Unbox Robotics’ $28 million round in January, Armatrix’s $2.1 million in February and Anscer Robotics’ Rs 45 crore Series A in May.
Meanwhile, policy support is also building. In August 2026, four SAMARTH centres had reached more than 2,700 industries and trained about 33,000 people in Industry 4.0 technologies. The National Manufacturing Mission announced in 2025 prioritises technology access and workforce readiness, while NITI Aayog’s roadmap names robotics, artificial intelligence and digital twins as manufacturing enablers.

company_description: Cyient Semiconductors will use the capital to scale custom-chip development, manufacturing access, and global growth.
article_title: Cyient Semiconductors bags $10M from GlobalFoundries
article_excerpt:
Cyient Semiconductors bags $10M from GlobalFoundries
Cyient Semiconductors will use the capital to scale custom-chip development, manufacturing access, and global growth.
Cyient Semiconductors has secured $10 million equity investment from GlobalFoundries, a global semiconductor manufacturer serving the data centre, automotive, and communications markets.
Hyderabad-headquartered Cyient said the investment carries the same pre-money valuation of $490 million as its recent financing led by Edelweiss, taking its combined post-money valuation to $510 million.
However, the announcement does not explain the calculation behind the combined valuation. The Edelweiss round in May involved approximately $10 million in equity from funds managed by EAAA India Alternatives and affiliated co-investors, alongside structured debt.
The freshly raised capital will be used to expand Cyient's turnkey custom application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) capabilities, accelerate custom silicon development, and improve long-term access to wafers, the silicon discs on which chips are manufactured.
Suman Narayan, Chief Executive Officer of Cyient Semiconductors, said the investment would help the company accelerate innovation, strengthen engineering capabilities, and scale global customer engagements. He described the funding as “a strong validation” of the opportunity for semiconductor innovation from India.
Cyient develops ASICs, chips designed for particular products or functions, as well as power-management products. Its capabilities span chip architecture, design, manufacturing coordination, packaging, testing and qualification. Its customers operate across the automotive, industrial, artificial intelligence, communications and data centre markets.
The company follows a fabless model, meaning it designs chips but relies on specialist manufacturers, known as foundries, to produce them. GlobalFoundries' (GF) involvement is significant in this respect. The companies had already established a channel partnership in August 2025 to provide customers with access to GF’s semiconductor manufacturing services and technologies.
Cyient has also been expanding its product portfolio. In April, it completed an $85 million majority investment in Kinetic Technologies, adding more than 250 power-management and related products, alongside established customer relationships and semiconductor intellectual property.
The latest investment comes amid growing interest in India’s chip-design sector. In February, Bengaluru-based C2i Semiconductors raised $15 million in a Series A round led by Peak XV Partners, while Vervesemi Microelectronics secured $10 million from investors including Ashish Kacholia and Unicorn India Ventures. Both companies are developing chips for applications spanning AI infrastructure, power management, and industrial systems.
However, semiconductor businesses typically require substantial research and development spending and longer periods to bring products to commercial scale, making sustained funding important.
Government support is also expanding. In July 2026, the Union Cabinet approved Semicon 2.0, with an outlay of Rs 1.275 lakh crore, covering chip design, manufacturing equipment and materials, fabrication plants, advanced packaging, research, and talent development.
In November, the government opened applications for support covering equipment and materials, new fabrication facilities, and semiconductor assembly and testing. Of the 12 projects approved under the first phase of the India Semiconductor Mission, five had commenced commercial production by October.

company_description: premium menswear label specialising in trousers and other bottomwear
article_title: The Pant Project bags Rs 109 Cr to accelerate retail expansion
article_excerpt:
The Pant Project bags Rs 109 Cr to accelerate retail expansion
The Pant Project is targeting a larger role in premium menswear after raising Rs 109 crore to expand retail outlets and develop new product categories.
The Pant Project, a premium menswear label specialising in trousers and other bottomwear, has raised Rs 109 crore in a Series B funding round led by Mirae Asset Venture Investments.
Existing investor Sorin Investments also participated, alongside family offices and angel investors including Anisha Saraf, B&K Securities, MGA Ventures and B2V Ventures. The company has also secured venture debt from Alteria Capital, with IndigoEdge advising on the equity transaction.
Founded by brothers Dhruv and Udit Toshniwal, The Pant Project began as a digital-first business focused on fit, fabric performance and comfort for Indian men. Its products include Malai Pants and Inklock No Fade Black Jeans, and it sells through its website, Myntra, Amazon and physical stores.
Sorin partner Mandar Dandekar said revenue had grown “more than 5x” since its Series A, alongside what he described as “industry-leading repeat rates.”
The new capital will help the company expand from 25 exclusive stores to more than 150 over the next two to three years. It also plans to widen its range to jeans, athleisure, meaning clothing suited to exercise and everyday use, and casualwear, while investing in retail technology to connect online and in-store shopping.
Chief executive officer Dhruv Toshniwal said its digital beginnings had provided “the data, the product knowledge and the brand equity to now go deep offline.”
The expansion highlights a wider shift among direct-to-consumer (D2C) brands, which sell directly to customers through their own channels. A recent report by WPP Media, Google and Elevation Capital, in partnership with Kantar, said brands need broader distribution to grow from around Rs 100 crore to Rs 500 crore in revenue.
A CMAI-1Lattice estimate projects India’s apparel market to grow from $96 billion in 2025 to $146 billion by 2029.
The Pant Project is entering a competitive funding market. Menswear brand Snitch raised $40 million in a Series B round led by 360 ONE Asset in June 2025. Meanwhile, House of Chikankari raised Rs 25 crore from Cap Alpha Ventures in April 2026 to expand its product range and physical presence.
On the manufacturing side, the government revised its textile production-linked incentive scheme in October 2025, widening eligible man-made-fibre apparel and fabric categories and easing investment requirements. The application window was subsequently extended through March 2026.

article_title: Peppermint Robotics bags Rs 100 Cr in pre-Series B funding round
article_excerpt:
Peppermint Robotics bags Rs 100 Cr in pre-Series B funding round
The startup, which makes autonomous cleaning robots, is backed by pi Ventures and Crane Venture Partners.
Peppermint Robotics, which makes autonomous cleaning robots, has raised Rs 100 crore (about $10.5 million) in a pre-Series B round led by pi Ventures and Crane Venture Partners. Asiana Fund also participated in the round.
The round involved fresh capital and secondary share transactions.
The money arrives on the back of rapid growth by Peppermint.
The Pune- and Austin-based startup said it doubled its revenue last year and grew nearly sixfold between FY24 and FY26. It last raised Rs 34 crore ($4 million) in a Series A round in April 2025. Peppermint has a presence in nine countries, with the US being its biggest market.
Founded in 2019 at the Society for Innovation and Entrepreneurship at IIT Bombay, the company's autonomous cleaning robots are deployed across a range of commercial and industrial environments, including factories, hospitals, airports, malls, warehouses, hotels and universities. Its machines scrub floors and move materials in factories, hospitals, airports, malls, warehouses, hotels and universities. They are designed to fit into existing routines rather than disrupt workflows.
The company primarily serves facility management companies that oversee cleaning operations, including the selection of equipment, chemicals and cleaning processes.
One of its more challenging deployments is at a global pharmaceutical company, where its cleanroom robots have passed qualification testing in an EU GMP Grade cleanroom, among the most tightly regulated settings a cleaning robot can enter, Peppermint said, in a statement.
Cleanroom robots are specialised manipulators engineered to operate in controlled, contamination-free environments.
The startup builds its hardware, software and perception systems in-house and assembles its robots in Pune. They run on proprietary Peppermint OS, using computer vision and LiDAR to map spaces, plan routes, and avoid obstacles. Operators can monitor them in real time through a cloud dashboard. For security-sensitive sites, the company offers fully offline 'stealth' robots that meet stringent information securtiy requirements.
Runal Dahiwade, Founder and CEO of Peppermint Robotics, said, "Cleaning teams keep hospitals, factories and airports running. Our robots work alongside them and take on the most repetitive, physically demanding jobs, like floor scrubbing and material transportation. Our customers judge us on one thing: a clean floor, every shift.
"So we build our robots heavy-duty, to last multiple years, and we stay with every machine for its whole lifecycle. This round lets us build more of them, closer to our customers worldwide."
The newly raised capital will go towards next-generation robotics and expanding manufacturing capacity. An assembly line in North America is also being planned over the coming months.
Peppermint also intends to step up business development in the United States and Asia, grow its presence in Europe, and hire senior leaders and engineers.
On the product side, it plans to widen its range of floor-cleaning and material-handling robots and develop its cleanroom line.
Investors are optimistic about Peppermint's potential and promise.
Shubham Sandeep, Partner at pi Ventures, pointed to the company's "clear ROI" in demanding settings such as healthcare and hospitality. Anandamoy Roychowdhary of Crane Venture Partners said Peppermint has built a production-grade cleanroom robot for mission-critical businesses. Neha Aggarwal of Asiana Fund called the company the kind of advanced manufacturing business India can build for global markets.
Edited by Swetha Kannan

company_description: Funds managed by Blackstone Private Equity will invest Rs 5,000 crore ($535 million) in compulsorily convertible preference shares.
article_title: IIFL Finance to raise Rs 6,414 Cr led by Blackstone
article_excerpt:
IIFL Finance to raise Rs 6,414 Cr led by Blackstone
Funds managed by Blackstone Private Equity will invest Rs 5,000 crore ($535 million) in compulsorily convertible preference shares.
IIFL Finance has approved a Rs 6,414 crore ($686 million) primary capital raise, with Blackstone leading the round.
The board cleared the preferential issue at a meeting on Tuesday. The deal is one of the largest primary private equity infusions in a listed Indian non-banking finance company, according to IIFL.
Funds managed by Blackstone Private Equity will invest Rs 5,000 crore ($535 million) in compulsorily convertible preference shares, which will convert into equity at Rs 602 a share, in line with the regulatory price, within 18 months of allotment. The company said this would give Blackstone a stake of about 16 % on a fully diluted basis.
The promoters, Nirmal Jain and R. Venkataraman, will invest Rs 1,264 crore (135 million) through a preferential allotment of warrants, and will continue as co-promoters. Anchorage Capital is also participating, with a Rs 150 crore (16 million) primary equity investment. The company and its promoters have signed definitive agreements with both investors.
IIFL Finance said the entire sum will go in as primary capital. On a pro forma basis for September 2026, which would lift its capital adequacy ratio from roughly 17% to roughly 30%. The company said the money would support growth in its secured lending businesses, particularly gold finance, and could, over time, improve its credit ratings and lower its borrowing costs.
Nirmal Jain, founder and managing director of IIFL Finance, said: “We are delighted to welcome Blackstone as a partner in IIFL Finance. Their investment is a strong endorsement of the franchise our team has built, and of the opportunity to bring formal, secured credit to millions of underserved households and small businesses across India. Venkat and I are investing Rs 1,264 crores alongside Blackstone, which reflects our own conviction in the Company’s next phase of growth.
“This partnership is about more than capital. Blackstone brings deep experience in building market-leading businesses in India, strong governance discipline, and a global perspective. The investment strengthens our balance sheet and gives us the headroom to scale our franchises, invest further in technology, and deepen our co-lending partnerships with banks, while staying disciplined on risk and capital.”
IIFL Finance also expects to draw on Blackstone’s global network and operational expertise, including in technology, data and artificial intelligence. Blackstone representatives are proposed to join the board, which the company said would strengthen governance while preserving its entrepreneurial culture.
Mukesh Mehta, chief investment officer for India private equity and senior managing director at Blackstone, said: “We are pleased to invest in IIFL Finance, a leading retail lending platform in India with a strong franchise and commitment to serving underserved customers. Building great businesses has been central to our approach over more than two decades of investing in India, and we look forward to partnering with Nirmal, Venkat and the management team to support IIFL Finance’s continued growth.”
The transaction remains subject to customary regulatory and shareholder approvals. Trilegal advised IIFL Finance, while Khaitan & Co advised Blackstone.
IIFL Finance offers gold, business, home and microfinance loans, among other products, through 5,091 branches across urban and rural India. Blackstone, which says it manages nearly $1.4 trillion in assets, has been investing in India for 20 years."

article_title: Matiks raises $10M in pre-Series A round led by General Catalyst
article_excerpt:
Matiks raises $10M in pre-Series A round led by General Catalyst
The company said it will use the funding to expand internationally, develop new games and social experiences, and launch an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered game creation platform that will enable users to build and publish games without writing code.
Bengaluru-based social gaming platform Matiks has raised $10 million in a pre-Series A funding round led by General Catalyst. The round also saw participation from entrepreneur Ronnie Screwvala and existing investors Info Edge Ventures, Tanglin Venture Partners, and Untitled Ventures.
According to a statement by the company, the fresh capital will be used to expand internationally, develop new games and social experiences, and launch an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered game creation platform that will enable users to build and publish games without writing code.
Founded in 2024, Matiks develops games centred on mathematics, memory, logic and puzzles, combining competitive gameplay with social features.
In September 2026, 2.2 million people played 48 million games on the platform. Its daily active users have more than doubled since June to over 300,000, with early engagement emerging in markets including Japan, the US and South Korea, the compamy said.
“Over the last decade, we have made it incredibly easy to consume content but have done far less to make using our brains equally entertaining. We started Matiks with a simple belief: using your brain can be just as fun and addictive as any other form of entertainment," said Sudhanshu Bhatia, co-founder and chief executive officer of Matiks.
"Our ambition is to make mind sports as culturally relevant as physical sports and esports - giving mental athletes, puzzlers, and competitive players the visibility, communities, and recognition they deserve. With AI, we want anyone, anywhere in the world, to create a brain game that millions can play. We are not trying to get people off their phones; we are trying to give them something better to do on them,” he added.
The company said users who complete a seven-day streak show 62% retention one month later, while some early cohorts have retained 32% of users at week 52. Its recently launched single-player puzzle format, SNAC, has also driven longer engagement, with sessions that include the format running approximately three times longer.
Rahul Humayan, partner at General Catalyst, said the platform was addressing demand for alternatives to conventional digital content.
"Negative content is consuming a growing share of our screen time, and Matiks is building the alternative: a social platform for brain games where people challenge friends, learn from one another and, soon, use AI to create games of their own. Sudhanshu, Sushant and Mohan have built one of the most engaged communities we have seen in consumer, from everyday players to world champions, and they are now taking it global. We are proud to partner with them as they make brain games a category of their own," he said.
Matiks will initially prioritise expansion in the US before entering other tier-one markets. It also plans to increase investments in engineering, AI, product, design, game development and growth, alongside scaling creator partnerships and global distribution.
The company plans to develop an AI-powered game creation engine that will allow users to create, publish and share brain games across multiple formats. It expects user-generated content to increase the variety of games available on the platform.

article_title: Sachin Tendulkar backs Hitwicket maker Metasports Interactive
article_excerpt:
Sachin Tendulkar backs Hitwicket maker Metasports Interactive
Sachin Tendulkar joins Hitwicket maker Metasports Interactive as a strategic investor, backing its ambition to reach 100 million downloads amid growing competition in India's gaming industry.
Metasports Interactive, the Hyderabad-based maker of cricket strategy game Hitwicket, has brought cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar on board as a strategic investor. He will also serve as the game’s brand ambassador.
Financial terms and valuation remain undisclosed.
Existing backers include venture-capital firms Prime Venture Partners and Singapore’s Horizon Ventures, as well as cricket commentator Harsha Bhogle.
This development is separate from the $20 million in user-acquisition funding it secured from London-based Metica in April. That earlier, non-dilutive facility was intended to fund marketing and international expansion without giving up equity.
Metasports has not specified how Tendulkar’s investment will be deployed. It aims to reach 100 million downloads within three years. The company claims Hitwicket has more than 20 million users across 120 countries, revenue doubled in the six months before the announcement, and players spend an average of 51 minutes daily on the game.
According to the company, more than 97% of its revenue comes from in-app purchases, or optional items bought within the game. Its wider ambition is to build mobile sports gaming franchises beyond cricket.
Hitwicket is a multiplayer strategy title that puts tactical decisions ahead of reflexes. Players manage a virtual side and choose how to approach each ball.
Tendulkar said it captures cricket’s strategic thinking, explaining that “Cricket has always involved reading the bowler, assessing the field and deciding the right approach for every ball.” He will also feature in the game and related content.
Reddy said Tendulkar’s cricketing knowledge would help the team understand elite players’ decisions and refine gameplay.
India’s gaming market offers a substantial audience, although converting it into globally competitive businesses and original intellectual property remains a challenge. The Game Developer Association of India estimates that the country had 511 million players and $1.04 billion in video-game revenue in 2025.
Recent funding deals demonstrate investor interest across genres. Bengaluru-based Spill Games raised $10.5 million in October, led by Elevation Capital, while social gaming platform Matiks raised $10 million led by General Catalyst. Cricket-focused LightFury Games also secured $11 million from investors including Blume Ventures, V3 Ventures, MIXI and Times Internet.
Policy is shifting too. The Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025, and its rules, effective from May 1, 2026, prohibit online money games while establishing a framework for e-sports and online social games, with user-safety and grievance-redressal requirements. Classification considers factors such as stakes, expected cash winnings and whether rewards can be converted outside a game.

article_title: Live2.ai raises Rs 130 Cr to expand its AI-led social commerce platform
article_excerpt:
Live2.ai raises Rs 130 Cr to expand its AI-led social commerce platform
The pre-Series B round, led by VC firm IvyCap Ventures, comprises fresh capital for business expansion and a secondary component for partial liquidity to early shareholders.
Bengaluru-based Live2.ai, which uses artificial intelligence (AI) to connect social-media intelligence with marketing and commerce, has raised Rs 130 crore ($14 million) in a pre-Series B funding round led by venture capital firm IvyCap Ventures.
The round combines fresh capital for business expansion and a secondary component that provides partial liquidity to early shareholders.
Live2.ai plans to invest the capital in its AI agent platform, expand enterprise deployments, strengthen cloud infrastructure across North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific, and recruit engineers, data scientists, and customer success staff.
“Brands today are drowning in signals and starved of action,” said J Venkat, Co-founder and Chief Executive Officer, Live2.ai. The funding, he added, would help bring detection, decision-making, and activation into a single governed workflow for global enterprise customers.
The platform monitors conversations across Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Reddit, X, and review websites. It integrates trend analysis, influencer-content audits, campaign publishing, and performance measurement. It also converts content cleared for commercial use into shoppable experiences across websites, retail outlets, customer relationship management systems, and online marketplaces.
The investment reflects a wider shift in how brands use social media to understand consumer behaviour and drive sales.
“Social has become a key channel for how consumers discover, evaluate, and buy, yet brands still rely on fragmented and manual tools to understand and act on it,” said Vikram Gupta, Founder and Managing Partner of IvyCap Ventures. He said Live2.ai was building an AI-native operating system to turn real-time cultural signals into commerce, with the security and governance required by global brands.
Co-founder and Chief Operating Officer Neha Suyal said the challenge is to turn intelligence into timely, measurable action at scale.
Live2.ai says it serves more than 200 brands across the United States, Europe and Southeast Asia, including Henkel’s Schwarzkopf, Titan Brands, and Shiseido. Revenue grew fourfold over the past 12 months, according to the company, with 90% generated outside India.
The investment comes at a time when funding into Indian AI businesses is growing. Recent rounds include voice-AI startup Navana.ai’s Rs 40 crore Series A fundraise in September and enterprise software company Kapture’s $10 million pre-Series B funding in June.
Policy is evolving alongside the industry. The government’s IndiaAI Mission has an outlay of Rs 10,371.92 crore over five years to develop computing infrastructure, support domestic AI capabilities, and promote responsible adoption.
Governance guidelines issued in February this year propose national institutions for AI policy coordination and safety. Separately, consumer-affairs guidance requires clear disclosure of paid or barter influencer endorsements.

article_title: Seeds Fincap secures over Rs 100 Cr in Series B led by Michael & Susan Dell Foundation
article_excerpt:
Seeds Fincap secures over Rs 100 Cr in Series B led by Michael & Susan Dell Foundation
Seeds Fincap said it plans to use the latest funding to open more physical branches, hire field workers, and upgrade its risk tracking tools as it expands further into rural and semi-urban towns.
Seeds Fincap Pvt Ltd, a non-baking financial company (NBFC) supporting small Indian businesses, has raised more than Rs 100 crore in its Series B funding round led by the Michael & Susan Dell Foundation.
Existing investors Z47 and Lok Capital also joined the round along with Norinchukin Capital and Alteria Capital. Unitus Capital served as the main financial adviser for the deal.
The company said it plans to use the latest funding to open more physical branches, hire field workers, and upgrade its risk tracking tools as it expands further into rural and semi-urban towns.
The new cash boost comes at a key moment for Seeds, as the team sets its sights on reaching Rs 1,000 crore in assets under management by March 2027.
Started in 2021 by Subhash Chandra Acharya, Avishek Sarkar, and Sumeet Dhall, Seeds caters to nano enterprises. These are small businesses that may have limited access to formal credit from banks. Instead of asking for traditional assets as proof, the company says it assesses the cash flows and operating activity of businesses when evaluating borrowers. It offers loans ranging from Rs 50,000 to Rs 10 lakh to small businesses and traders.
"We are delighted to welcome the Michael & Susan Dell Foundation as the lead investor in our Series B round," said Subhash Chandra Acharya, MD & CEO of Seeds Fincap.
"Their participation is a strong endorsement of the impact we seek to create. The continued support from our existing investors reflects their sustained confidence in our business model and the strength of our portfolio. This capital will enable us to deepen our footprint, strengthen our technology capabilities, and reach more underserved entrepreneurs."
The firm reported a profit in both FY25 and FY26. It disbursed around Rs 620 crore in loans during FY26, while its assets under management stood at Rs 722 crore as of August 2026. Its network had expanded to 164 branches across India, with more than 70,000 active borrowers.
Rakesh Goyal, Head of Financial Services in India at the Michael & Susan Dell Foundation, said small business owners often face challenges in accessing formal credit. He said Seeds combines local market knowledge with risk assessment practices to serve this segment.
Anish Patil, Principal at Z47, which backed the company at an early stage, said the investment was based on the founders’ experience in small-business lending. He said the company had expanded its loan book over the past three years while maintaining its approach to credit and risk management.

article_title: Bharat Semi raises $24M to develop AI-enabled sensors
article_excerpt:
Bharat Semi raises $24M to develop AI-enabled sensors
Bharat Semi has raised seed funding to develop programmable AI-powered sensors, targeting the growing demand for intelligent, energy-efficient hardware for robotics, vehicles and other machines.
India- and US-based semiconductor company Bharat Semi has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop programmable smart sensors for Physical AI, where machines use artificial intelligence to perceive and act in the real world.
The round was led by Info Edge, the internet group behind Naukri; South Park Commons, a founder community and early-stage investor; and IndusBridge Ventures, which backs deeptech sector.
Micromax, an electronics group; Valour Capital, a deeptech investor; New York-based venture syndicate Gaingels and angel investors Mukul Agarwal and Kartik Iyer also participated.
The funding will accelerate product development, expand the US engineering team and support efforts to secure global customers.
Founded in 2021, Bharat Semi operates across New Delhi, Bengaluru and San Francisco. It is initially targeting consumer electronics and surveillance, with potential longer-term applications in robotics, vehicles, drones, aerospace and defence.
Its sensors combine data capture and AI processing in a single component. A camera-equipped device could interpret an image at the point of capture, rather than send raw data to a separate processor or cloud server. This is known as edge inference, where AI processes information close to its source, potentially reducing delays and energy consumption.
Bharat Semi said its technology could reduce data movement between components by up to 99% and lower system costs by up to ten times compared with conventional multi-chip systems.
“Soon, growth in the sensor market will be driven by capturing data for machines,” co-founder Vinayak Dalmia said, arguing that sensing, processing and software must be designed together.
Co-founder Vrinda Kapoor described the shift as “intelligence at the right place”, saying it offered India an opportunity to build globally relevant technology businesses.
The technical team also includes Boyd Fowler, former chief technology officer of image-sensor maker OmniVision.
The investment comes as AI moves beyond data centres and into physical devices and machines. Bharat Semi has reportedly secured design wins with US defence company General Atomics and India's Kaynes Semicon.
Other Indian deeptech ventures have attracted funding this year. Bengaluru-based chipmaker C2i Semiconductors raised $15 million in February, while sensor and navigation technology developer Yaanendriya secured Rs 15 crore in July. Physical AI startup Flo Mobility raised $2.5 million in May to expand its construction robotics business.
Policy support is also expanding. Approved in July 2026 with an outlay of Rs 1,27,500 crore, India’s Semicon 2.0 programme covers chip design, manufacturing equipment and materials, fabrication, packaging, research and talent development. In November, the government reported that five of 12 approved semiconductor projects had commenced commercial production.

A FIRE score reviews their finances across three areas: whether savings are on track, whether investments are growing efficiently, and how well a portfolio could cope with personal or market shocks.

Prospective clients can book a free 45-minute one-to-one session with a SEBI-registered adviser to spot weaknesses in their finances and agree next steps. BankSocial , a provider of Web3 and AI-powered financial technology, has partnered with Vyrdia , a core processor and digital technology provider to credit unions and community financial institutions, to bring embedded wealth, payments and fraud prevention tools to credit unions.

Because the referral frameworks are already aligned, participating institutions can enable these services without replacing their existing core systems.

Prospera, BankSocial’s WealthTech solution, enables members to buy fractional shares, ETFs, IRAs and digital assets directly through their credit union’s mobile app. The technology is designed to help credit unions retain deposits and member investment activity within their own platforms.

Remint provides payment infrastructure, routing transactions across FedNow, RTP and stable-value settlement channels. The company says this can help reduce payment friction and transaction costs.

Meanwhile, Secura and Substrate provide security and AI capabilities, combining real-time transaction monitoring and preventative fraud controls with AI agent orchestration designed around financial compliance requirements.

The agreement comes as credit unions develop their 2027 strategies around member wealth retention and digital transformation. By bringing BankSocial’s services into Vyrdia’s existing ecosystem, the companies aim to simplify vendor assessment and integration for participating institutions.

Its platform covers digital identity and onboarding through Verifiied, domestic and cross-border payments through Remint, wealth and digital asset services through Prospera and fraud resilience through Secura.

The company also operates Nuron, an employee API layer, the Axon API layer and Substrate, an AI operating system. BankSocial’s technology is designed to connect traditional financial services with distributed ledger technology while enabling credit unions and community banks to launch digital services.

Vyrdia provides core processing and technology services to credit unions and community financial institutions, with a focus on flexible and scalable digital banking infrastructure.

article_title: Sanctuary Wealth lands $250m to fund advisor succession
article_excerpt:
Sanctuary Wealth has received a $250m growth capital commitment from its existing backer Kennedy Lewis Investment Management.

The deal hands Sanctuary a larger pool of money to finance the ambitions, equity sales and succession plans of the firms on its platform.

The fresh funding will be used to widen the specialist expertise available to Sanctuary’s Partner Firms, helping them serve clients across a broader range of needs, win new business and complete acquisitions.

Sanctuary will also gain more room to supply capital directly to Partner Firm owners, whether they want to fund expansion, cash out part of their stake or get ready for a leadership handover.

Kennedy Lewis, a multi-strategy private credit manager overseeing roughly $40bn in assets, has structured its commitment as $50m in mandatory convertible debt alongside a $200m delayed-draw term loan.

In addition, the investor has chosen to turn its current outstanding convertible debt holding in Sanctuary into equity. The relationship between the two firms dates back to 2022, and since that first investment Sanctuary has doubled its count of Partner Firms and nearly tripled the assets on its platform.

Sanctuary’s network has grown to 125 Partner Firms, representing $71bn in assets either on the platform or currently moving onto it. The firm has completed 13 minority investments in its Partner Firms so far.

Over eight years, Sanctuary has built a platform designed to help advisors leaving wirehouses establish their own independent businesses. Its scale and depth have drawn growing attention from advisors and independent wealth managers, prompting the company to introduce additional affiliation models that give sophisticated advisors greater choice in how they pursue their goals.

A dedicated committee of Sanctuary’s Board reviewed and negotiated competing financing proposals before settling on the Kennedy Lewis deal. Completion is anticipated in the first quarter of 2027, pending standard closing conditions, including the end of the relevant waiting period under the Hart Scott Rodino Act and approval from FINRA.

Sanctuary Wealth CEO Adam Malamed said, “Sanctuary’s platform was built to help wirehouse advisors become independent, deepen relationships with their clients and build enterprise value in firms of their own. That heritage remains central to Sanctuary’s identity and growth strategy. As our Partner Firms continue to evolve, this new capital enhances our ability to invest in what they need as established businesses, giving them more ways to grow and their owners more options for realizing the value they have created.”

Sanctuary Wealth co-presidents Vince Fertitta and Robert Walter remarked, “Our Partner Firms are our clients, and we have to earn their business every day. After years of helping advisors build enterprise value in their firms, we want them to have more ways to put that value to work. Founders should be able to monetize their businesses on their own timeline by selling a minority or majority stake and keep leading the business on the same independent terms that made ownership so attractive to them in the first place.”

Malamed added, “Sanctuary carefully considered the best path forward for this new phase of our evolution and chose to expand our relationship with Kennedy Lewis. Kennedy Lewis understands our business and is completely aligned with our focus on helping our Partner Firms achieve their full potential. We look forward to continuing this constructive relationship and working together to capture Sanctuary’s long-term opportunity.”

article_title: Hoxton Wealth ends self-funded era with $135m deal

Hoxton Wealth , a London and Dubai-based international wealth management platform built around technology, has secured a $135m commitment from Aspirity Partners I, marking the end of its self-funded journey and the first outside capital to enter the business since 2018.

The strategic minority investment will fund a more aggressive yet measured growth push. Hoxton plans to widen its international footprint, hire senior wealth advisers and complete a number of targeted acquisitions. Alongside these moves, the firm will keep investing in the platform, internal processes and standard of service it delivers to clients.

Aspirity sizes this market at roughly $1.2 trillion in assets, noting that just 25% of it is currently advised and that it has long-term structural growth behind it.

For Aspirity, the deal fits within its Financial Technology & Services strategy. The investor had already flagged international wealth management as a priority area through its Proactive Thematic Origination programme, pointing to the rise in cross-border wealth and the growing complexity facing globally mobile clients.

The partnership grew out of a bilateral process that unfolded over close to twelve months. During that period, Aspirity worked directly with founder Chris Ball and his team to shape an arrangement tailored to Hoxton’s ambitions, drawing partly on input from several Aspirity Innovators and Leaders.

Hoxton Wealth founder and CEO Chris Ball said, “Taking external capital for the first time is an important moment for Hoxton, so choosing the right partner mattered enormously. The fact that Aspirity are so deliberate in their strategy it was obvious they had unusual depth of knowledge on the market, and informed perspectives on how they may be able to support our plans.

“This partnership gives us the capital and support to build sustainably for the long term. We can bring more experienced advisers into the business, expand our international reach with discipline, continue strengthening our senior leadership and processes, and pursue the acquisition opportunities already in front of us.”

article_title: Curvestone AI expands compliance automation across 350 firms
article_excerpt:
Curvestone AI, an artificial intelligence-powered compliance platform for regulated financial services, has partnered with Connect for Intermediaries to introduce automated compliance reviews across the network’s more than 350 member firms.

The deployment is designed to replace traditional sample-based checks with comprehensive case-file reviews, enabling firms to assess every case rather than examining only a proportion of their business. Curvestone AI says this approach can help financial services firms reduce compliance risks, increase processing capacity and support business growth without proportionately increasing staffing requirements. Each reviewed case also generates an audit trail to support regulatory oversight.

The partnership includes integration with OMS, the customer relationship management (CRM) system used by Connect. By linking Curvestone AI directly with the platform, compliance teams can avoid manually transferring case information between systems. The integration is also expected to enable advisers to conduct preliminary checks before submitting cases for formal compliance review.

Curvestone AI automates compliance processes across regulated financial services, including case-file assessments, financial promotions reviews and financial crime controls. Its platform serves mortgage brokers, intermediary networks, lenders and wealth advisers across the UK.

The initial deployment represents the first phase of the partnership, with the companies planning further enhancements following the wider roll-out.

Curvestone AI founder and CEO Dawid Kotur said, “This partnership with Connect perfectly demonstrates the network use case for our proposition and shows how by using us via a CRM system like OMS, we can save both the network and AR valuable time without sacrificing quality and overall compliance.”

He added, “This is the first phase of our on-going work with Connect and we look forward to being able to announce enhancements in the coming months as the roll-out finishes.”

Connect for Intermediaries CEO Liz Syms said the network must review mortgage and protection cases submitted by its member firms, with a comprehensive manual file check typically taking two to three hours, depending on complexity.

“Using Curvestone has brought that down to minutes, allowing our team to spend more time on high-value items such as coaching and training. In addition, the integration with OMS has improved that efficiency even further, as it saves the team having to transfer the information into Curvestone’s own system. Going forward, the OMS integration will also facilitate the ability for advisers to do pre-checks of their own before cases are sent to compliance for file reviews.”.

article_title: Nagaris secures A$1.26m seed for AI accounting platform
article_excerpt:
Nagaris , a platform built to run Australian accounting practices, has completed a seed equity round worth A$1.26m, backed in part by the partners behind AI-native accounting firm BPAG Accountants.

The partners of the five practices that combined to create BPAG took part in the round. They were joined by several other accounting firms, a group of private investors and the founder of Nagaris. Best Practice Group helped arrange the investment.

The round closed in August 2026 and was made up entirely of ordinary shares. Nagaris plans to put the capital towards developing its product further.

The company points to BPAG as evidence that its technology delivers. The firm was created when five practices came together: Proactive Business Services in Sydney, CP Partners and BPAG Epping in Melbourne, Palacc near Canberra, and PBS Accountants & Advisers in Adelaide. The combined business now operates from four offices, serves thousands of clients and uses Nagaris to run the entire practice.

Within the platform, an assistant called Ask Nagaris draws on more than 80 specialist skills to produce first drafts of everyday tasks, including BAS workpapers, Division 7A calculations, research notes and letters to clients. Because the system creates workpapers directly from a client’s Xero data, a BAS that once demanded over 90 minutes of preparation can now be reviewed and approved in around 10 minutes, though more complicated returns take longer. Every output is checked and approved by a qualified accountant, and no material is sent to clients or the ATO without human sign-off. Over a fortnight, 54 BPAG staff used the assistant close to 2,000 times.

Nagaris also produces the Nagaris AI Accounting Index, which grades AI models against 112 questions on Australian accounting, and routes each query to whichever model configuration performs strongest. In addition to BPAG, a further 50 accounting firms are using the platform.

Founded in 2025 and headquartered in Sydney, Nagaris offers Australian accountants a single client file that brings together proposals, AML/CTF checks, e-signing, client queries, phone calls, SMS, meeting notes, internal chat, BAS workpapers and documents, with Ask Nagaris operating across all of these under the firm’s approval.

Nagaris founder Robert Coorey said, “Plenty of people are describing what an AI-native accounting firm might look like. BPAG is one: five firms, four offices, one client file, and a person signing off everything the software drafts.”

article_title: Marble raises $11m seed to finance AI compute
article_excerpt:
Marble , a capital markets firm focused on frontier markets and AI infrastructure finance, has come out of stealth with $11m in seed funding to build out its institutional trading and private credit operations.

Polychain Capital led the round. Maven 11, Ripple, Susquehanna Crypto, Lattice and Blockwall also took part, along with other venture and strategic backers and a small group of angel investors with an AI focus.

The company runs two divisions. Marble Compute is developing private credit infrastructure that links institutional lenders with neoclouds and GPU operators expanding AI capacity. Marble Markets is creating a platform where institutions can trade digital assets, real-world assets, prediction markets and compute, with Marble acting as counterparty.

Marble Compute is aimed at smaller, independent operators. The biggest listed neoclouds can raise money through public markets and major banks, but mid-market players often struggle to secure financing even when buyers have already committed to their capacity.

Marble Compute intends to originate, underwrite and structure deals for these businesses and present them to lenders through both conventional and on-chain credit structures. Its underwriting will look at the hardware, the credit quality of contracted customers and whether the operator can service its debt. Pending regulatory approval, the firm plans to fund deals through single-opportunity vehicles first, then move to multi-opportunity funds, all run through one asset management platform.

Marble Markets’ plans include compute forwards, which let operators fix a rental price now for capacity they will supply later. The firm is also developing spot trading, lending and derivatives for digital assets, block trading in prediction markets and over-the-counter compute forwards. Further ahead, it hopes to add tokenised equities and equity swaps, again subject to regulatory approval. To free up capital, clients will be able to post eligible digital and traditional assets held at participating custodians and brokerages as collateral, rather than prefunding trades with each counterparty.

Polychain Capital partner Angelo Goepel said, “Matt and Leon have built and run institutional trading and lending businesses at scale through multiple market cycles, and they understand market structure from the inside.

“That experience positions Marble to compete in two of the largest opportunities of this decade: bringing institutional trading to frontier markets and building the credit markets that AI infrastructure needs. We’re excited to lead Marble’s seed.”

Marble co-founder and co-CEO Leon Marshall said, “Two GPU operators can buy identical hardware and raise very different amounts of debt against it. A lender wants to know who’s buying the compute, at what price and for how long.

“We’re bringing buyers, operators and lenders together so operators can secure customers for their capacity, lock in pricing on the share they want to hedge and raise financing against those cash flows. That gives lenders a clearer basis for deciding how much they can lend and operators a clearer view of how much equity they’ll need to build the next cluster.”

Marble co-founder and co-CEO Matt Ballensweig said, “Institutions want exposure to the markets that will define the next decade, from prediction markets to AI compute, but the liquidity and credit in those markets are still fragmented. Marble brings the trading and financing infrastructure institutions rely on to the markets they actually want to be in.”

article_excerpt:
Birmingham-based FinTech Lovey has secured a senior secured credit facility of up to £250m from alternative asset manager Pollen Street Capital, marking the largest funding line in the SME lender’s history.

The facility comprises £50m in committed capital and a £200m accordion, giving Lovey additional capacity to expand lending from its own balance sheet while continuing to grow its brokerage operations.

The funding will support the company’s efforts to increase its lending capacity and provide more UK small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) with access to credit. Lovey said the deal reflects institutional investor confidence in its lending model, technology and long-term growth plans.

Founded by Jack Smith in 2016, Lovey has grown from a one-person operation into a business employing 120 people. The company has provided more than £600m in loans to over 11,000 SMEs across the UK, targeting businesses seeking faster and more flexible access to finance.

Lovey entered direct lending in 2022, building on its experience as a broker to address gaps in the SME finance market. It now operates both models, allowing businesses to borrow directly from Lovey or access funding through its network of lending partners. The company says businesses can submit an enquiry in 60 seconds and may receive funds within four hours.

The new facility follows funding arrangements announced last year, including a £35m revolving credit facility from Paragon Bank and a £10m junior medium-term note programme from LGB Capital Markets.

Ashurst Perkins Coie advised Lovey on the transaction, while Simmons & Simmons represented Pollen Street. Founded in 2013, Pollen Street manages more than €9bn across private equity and credit strategies and employs over 100 professionals.

Lovey founder and CEO Jack Smith said, “This new facility is an important milestone for us and will enable us to put more capital behind UK small businesses, scale our own-book lending and give more SMEs access to finance when they need it. Pollen Street shares our belief that finances for small businesses should be simpler, faster and more flexible, and we’re really pleased to have them backing Lovey for this next stage of growth.”

Lovey chief operating officer Kai Hunter added, “The funding announced today is the result of close and collaborative work with Pollen Street and I am grateful to their team, and to our own, for the diligence they brought to it. This funding deepens our lending capacity and allows us to offer larger loans, so that we can back more of the UK’s small and medium-sized businesses, from those that have found finance hardest to secure to the well-established, with greater speed and certainty.”

Pollen Street investment director Ethan Saggu also commented, “Lovey has spent almost a decade seeing the UK SME lending market from a broker’s perspective, giving the team an expert view of where demand for credit is going unmet. We have financed a number of specialist SME lenders and recognise what it takes to grow from brokerage into balance-sheet lending. Lovey has done so with a well-defined product and a focused approach, and we look forward to supporting the team as it scales.”

Marble , a Paris-based fraud detection and anti-money laundering (AML) compliance platform, has secured €6.5m in Series A funding as it looks to make AI-driven automation more widely used by mid-market banks and FinTechs, according to EU-Startups.

Smartfin , a European venture capital and private equity firm backing high-growth B2B technology businesses, led the investment. ADNEXUS also joined the round, alongside existing investors Passion, 42Capital and Hexa. The funding brings Marble’s total raised to €9m, with TSIC also among its existing investors.

Marble will use the funding to embed AI more deeply into compliance workflows and shorten deployment times at banks and FinTechs. The company has identified four priorities: AI-powered automation, faster deployment, agentic compliance and adaptable systems.

This includes applying AI to rule creation, alert triage and case investigation, alongside on-premises deployments that connect to a bank’s existing data rather than requiring months of transformation work. Marble is also developing native AI agents restricted to the data they are authorised to access.

The company also wants to turn rule and workflow updates into routine configuration work for compliance officers, reducing the need to launch a new technology project for each change.

Arnaud Schwartz and Pascal Delange, both former executives at French FinTech Shine, founded Marble in 2021. They said their experience managing financial crime compliance at Shine showed them that existing tools often added another layer of complexity rather than reducing manual work.

Marble’s no-code platform allows compliance and risk teams to create their own transaction monitoring rules without relying on vendors or IT departments. It also supports sanctions and watchlist screening, investigations and reporting, customer risk scoring and A/B testing of rules against live data.

The platform can be deployed on-premises or as SaaS, while its open-source core gives auditors visibility into how decisions are reached. Marble says the platform protects more than 3bn transactions annually and reduces manual review work by 90%.

The company reports that its platform is now deployed at more than 100 institutions across over 25 countries. Nearly 70% of its customers are based outside France, while 70% adopted Marble to replace an existing solution.

Marble is targeting more than €5m in annual recurring revenue by 2027 as it seeks to make automated, AI-powered compliance a standard part of financial crime operations.

Smartfin partner Saumitra Dubey said, “Marble makes automation the default, on the customer’s own infrastructure. Our conviction is that Marble becomes the structurally differentiated, modern financial crime operating system for mid-market banks and fintechs. That’s why we led this round.”

Marble CEO and co-founder Arnaud Schwartz said, “Compliance teams shouldn’t have to choose between staying compliant and moving fast. That’s exactly what we built Marble to solve. As the regulatory bar keeps rising, compliance teams are expected to do more with the same headcount. Our job is to make sure that it is Marble that absorbs that complexity and not our customers.”

Passion Capital partner Will Orde said, “More than 100 institutions now run Marble in production. When conviction meets execution like that, it’s simple: you lean in.”

article_title: Fin.com’s $20m bet on rebuilding cross-border payments
article_excerpt:
Fin.com , a financial infrastructure company building a unified network for global money movement, has emerged from stealth with $20m after quietly growing its annual recurring revenue more than 50-fold since the start of the year.

Until today, the company had never published a blog post, given an interview or publicly confirmed its own existence, despite its technology already moving money for some of the world’s largest payments and money-transfer platforms, leading prediction markets and major digital-asset exchanges, reaching 825 million users worldwide through those customers.

The $20m seed round was led by Expa and Uber co-founder Garrett Camp, with participation from Coinbase Ventures, Tenet Fund, Figure’s founders, Mesh founder Bam Azizi, Second Sight Ventures, and sovereign and royal family offices across the Gulf and Africa.

Cross-border money movement remains reliant on an ageing patchwork of bank messaging systems, local payment rails, intermediaries and manual processes. SWIFT, which has underpinned international bank messaging since the 1970s, was never built as a settlement network, and the gap shows up in fees, FX markups and settlement windows that can run for days.

Last year, $195 trillion moved across borders through rails like it, shedding cost and speed at every step. Fintech has spent a decade polishing the user experience sitting on top of that plumbing, while the infrastructure underneath stayed fragmented.

Fin.com was built to replace that plumbing directly. The company runs a single orchestration layer that allows businesses to collect, convert and move money internationally through local payment rails, USD virtual accounts, SWIFT, stablecoin settlement, liquidity and compliance, all within one network.

It holds licences and regulatory approvals that let it operate in markets many global providers find hard to reach, deliberately concentrating on the Middle East, Africa, South Asia and Southeast Asia, where cross-border flows remain especially fragmented.

Its approach to expansion is also unconventional. Rather than raising large sums to break into new markets from outside, Fin.com acquires licensed, established local operators and folds them into its network, a private equity-style playbook executed at venture pace. Buying into existing licences, banking relationships and local expertise lets the company plug new markets straight into its wider infrastructure.

Seven acquisitions have closed so far, with twelve targeted by the end of the year. That strategy has produced a company of more than 200 people across six offices in New York, Las Vegas, Dubai, Dhaka, Bangalore and Lahore, which has already processed billions in payment volume across more than 51 countries, with most transactions settling within minutes.

Fin.com has also built an advisory board drawing on senior figures from across payments and fintech, including Michael Tannenbaum of Figure, Imran Ahmad of Bitso, Matt Heiman of Mercury, Bruce Wallace of Revolut, former Binance board director Christy Choi, and Mesh founder Bam Azizi.

The company was co-founded by Nabeel Alamgir, a Forbes 30 Under 30 honoree and founder of Lunchbox, and Mustafa Dar, founder of 24/7 Jet and a venture partner at Expa, both of whom have personally experienced the cost and friction of sending money across borders.

The new capital will fund expansion into additional payment corridors and further acquisitions, and Fin.com is also targeting a bank acquisition within the next six months.

The extension drew backing from a broad group of strategic investors, including BNP Paribas, Bpifrance, Broadridge, Canton Foundation, Coinbase Ventures, DRW Venture Capital, Nasdaq Ventures, Royal Bank of Canada, Stellar and Susquehanna Private Equity Investments. Kaiko’s principal business supplies institutional-grade market data covering digital assets, while its data infrastructure arm extends this into onchain capital markets, supplying proprietary pricing data to smart contracts, converting onchain activity into standardised off-chain data, and supporting confidential valuation and analytics work.

article_title: Chift lands €10.5m to connect Europe’s fragmented finance
article_excerpt:
Chift , a European financial data connectivity platform, and a specialist integrator of accounting and business software for small and medium sized enterprises, has raised €10.5m in a Series A funding round.

The round was led by BlackFin Capital Partners, a private equity firm focused on the European FinTech sector, with participation from existing investors Entourage, Shapers, Seeder Fund and Wallonie Entreprendre.

The company was founded on the premise that financial data across Europe remains locked within thousands of disconnected national systems, preventing software providers from scaling across borders and stopping AI tools from gaining a full view of a business’s finances.

Chift’s founders spent years manually linking individual software tools for small businesses before deciding a broader, unified approach was needed.

Chift points to two developments reshaping its market: the rollout of e-invoicing mandates across Europe, which will push every business onto digital finance systems by 2030, and the rise of AI agents in accounting, which depend on connected data to function.

The company estimates that around 30 million small and medium sized businesses across Europe and the UK, alongside a €174bn accounting services sector that remains largely manual, will need their financial systems linked together in the coming years.

Chift operates a single integration that links software providers to more than 120 financial systems spanning the continent, with new connections added on an ongoing basis. The firm holds a leading position in France, Belgium and the Netherlands, entered Spain a year ago and is now expanding into the UK, the Nordics and Germany.

The new capital will fund development of an agentic layer that lets integrations configure themselves automatically and allows AI systems to act safely on financial data.

Chift also intends to extend its coverage into Spain, the UK, the Nordics, Germany and Italy over the coming years, while working to reach small businesses through the software providers, accountants and partners they already use. article_excerpt:
Settle , an inventory financing provider for consumer and ecommerce brands, has agreed a forward-flow arrangement with structured credit platform 3Jane that could unlock up to $100m in capital, a deal that puts stablecoin liquidity behind mainstream merchant lending.

Under the deal, 3Jane will commit $50m of capacity at the outset, and that figure can grow to $100m. 3Jane has already bought $18m of loans from Settle’s existing book and will keep acquiring qualifying new loans as Settle writes them.

The arrangement matters because of how it recycles capital. Each time Settle sells loans to 3Jane, it releases funds that can go straight into new originations. This lets Settle lend more without having to carry every loan on its own balance sheet.

Settle’s model fills the gap between paying for stock and selling it. The company settles supplier invoices and inventory bills on behalf of brands at the point of purchase. Brands then pay Settle back over time, either through longer payment windows or a set schedule of instalments. To date, Settle has deployed more than $4bn across thousands of consumer and ecommerce businesses.

3Jane channels capital to FinTech lenders through a conduit that is revolving, divided into tranches and built on blockchain infrastructure. Its pitch is that originators can access the economics of a private, unrated securitisation without each one having to build and pay for its own dedicated programme, a cost that often puts such structures beyond the reach of smaller lenders.

Settle CEO and founder Alek Koenig said, “Our customers need to pay for inventory before they can sell it. The forward flow with 3Jane gives us a more capital-efficient way to finance that gap at scale.”

3Jane CEO Jacob Chudnovsky added, “Settle has built a lending business serving thousands of consumer brands. 3Jane uses stablecoin liquidity to finance those loans through a structure designed to lower Settle’s financing costs.”

Fission , a blockchain-powered FinTech firm developing liquidity infrastructure for tokenised investment funds, has secured $10m in a Series A round as it seeks to bring faster access to capital to digital private markets.

The company argues that while tokenisation is shifting private-market funds onto digital rails, liquidity has lagged behind. Tokenisation has reshaped how fund interests are issued, distributed and settled. However, much of the surrounding market structure has stayed the same, and investors in tokenised funds still face periodic redemption windows, thin secondary markets and restrictive financing arrangements.

Fission aims to address this by letting eligible holders of supported tokenised fund products access capital without having to wait for conventional redemption cycles. Its coverage spans asset classes such as private credit, alternatives and other institutional investment products. Fission has already handled millions of dollars in redemptions, which it says reflects rising demand for more flexible liquidity. It is increasing its capacity by drawing on both traditional and on-chain capital sources.

The platform has been designed specifically for institutional and permissioned markets. Its infrastructure accounts for the investor eligibility rules, transfer restrictions and compliance obligations that apply to regulated investment products. This enables Fission to offer on-chain liquidity while keeping in place the safeguards demanded by securities markets.

Fission’s mission is to make investment funds more liquid, accessible and financeable by providing the digital infrastructure needed for these products to scale worldwide.

Fission founder and CEO Jonathan Shaffer said, “Putting funds on-chain is only the beginning. The real promise of tokenization is creating fundamentally better markets around these assets: broader distribution, continuous liquidity and the ability to use fund interests as collateral in lending markets. Pantera Capital general partner Franklin Bi said, “Investment funds are moving onto digital rails and liquidity is one of the critical pieces required for that transition to reach its full potential. article_title: Iridium Credit raises $3m to verify every invoice
article_excerpt:
Iridium Credit , a provider of verification infrastructure for the invoice finance market, has secured $3m in a funding round jointly led by Field Ventures and MGV.

The company uses agentic technology to check each invoice a lender finances against its supporting documentation, confirm it with the debtor, and track it all the way through collections and cash posting. Iridium says this approach makes reviewing a lender’s entire book less expensive than manually reviewing only a portion of it.

According to Iridium, gaps in manual verification have held back invoice finance in the US. The practice, in which a business sells an unpaid invoice to a lender at a discount in exchange for immediate cash, accounts for just 2% of US GDP. By comparison, it reaches 14% in Chile, which benefits from a government e-invoicing registry.

The firm attributes this gap to the difficulty of confirming that invoices are genuine. Manual checks cost a factor roughly $22 in staff time per invoice, meaning only around 20% of invoices are verified, and smaller invoices are frequently left unfunded. A common workaround, confirming that an invoice appears on the debtor’s ledger, can take between two and three weeks and does not involve reviewing the underlying paperwork.

Unchecked invoices have created exposure running into billions of dollars. Iridium pointed to First Brands, which when it filed for bankruptcy in September 2025, it held $2.3bn in factoring liabilities. Point Bonita Capital, part of Jefferies’ Leucadia Asset Management, had been factoring First Brands invoices owed by retailers such as Walmart, AutoZone and O’Reilly, and reported exposure of around $715m. A court-appointed examiner concluded that lenders purchasing these receivables generally did not view the original invoices or cross-check the data against those in First Brands’ own database.

Iridium’s platform processes whichever documents accompany an invoice, such as a rate confirmation and bill of lading in freight, a timesheet in staffing, or a purchase order for product businesses, and confirms that amounts, dates and parties match. It compares each invoice against the lender’s full funding history to identify duplicates submitted under new numbers or loads billed twice. Debtor confirmation requests are sent white-labelled under the lender’s or client’s name. Costs are reduced because the checks are run agentically instead of through staff hours, while the model adapts to industry-specific fraud patterns, meaning a freight portfolio and a staffing portfolio are assessed differently.

Any invoice that fails a check is escalated to a human reviewer, with the discrepancy flagged and source documents attached. A record of every check, contact and decision is kept with the invoice for the lender’s bank, auditors or credit committee. The platform sits on top of existing lender workflows, integrating with FactorSoft and FactorCloud so that lenders can continue using their current systems.

The new capital will support the rollout of Iridium across US invoice finance lenders and the development of its payment intelligence network. This cross-industry layer of verification and payment data is designed to detect fraud that individual lenders cannot spot alone, and to support the banks, private credit funds and vertical platforms entering the market.

The company plans to use the capital to grow its international footprint, strengthen its position in priority overseas markets and speed up work on the autonomous features of its platform.

Finite State aims to let more manufacturers worldwide spot the mismatch between the software they intend to ship and the code that actually ends up running on a finished device, while continually detecting and reducing risk across supply chains that keep growing more complex.

The raise lands at a critical moment for product security. In October, AI-driven research exposed serious weaknesses in heavily used software, among them a flaw in the PHP programming language, which supports a large share of the web. Security leaders have labelled this wave of discoveries the “Vulnpocalypse.”

Artificial intelligence has cut the window between discovering a weakness and weaponising it from weeks down to days, and occasionally hours. Connected hardware faces particular danger, as one defect in a widely shared open source component can be embedded across millions of products that are difficult to catalogue and slow to update. Manufacturers now face a different challenge: identifying which of their products carry a given flaw.

Regulators are adding pressure at the same time. Authorities across the globe increasingly require connected products to be secure by design, with protections proven before release rather than bolted on later.

Frameworks including the EU Cyber Resilience Act, FDA premarket cybersecurity rules, UNECE R155 and R156 for vehicles, and IEC 62443 for industrial systems all make manufacturers responsible for demonstrating compliance. Failure can bring restricted market access, recalls and legal liability.

Compliance is hard because modern devices are built from many parts rather than written from a blank page.

One product may combine open source libraries, third-party components and older code from multiple suppliers, and the final firmware frequently departs from what the source code and bill of materials suggest. Without visibility, manufacturers cannot protect their products.

Finite State’s AI-powered platform inspects the software and firmware within finished devices, showing manufacturers exactly what sits inside the goods they produce and sell. Its coverage stretches from vehicles and medical devices to industrial machinery, consumer electronics and essential utility infrastructure.

The technology detects both known weaknesses and zero-day vulnerabilities, then helps manufacturers remediate the exploitable ones ahead of any attack.

Its clients cover critical infrastructure and the wider connected device landscape, including national power grids, a US national security research laboratory, global carmakers, life-saving medical equipment makers and producers of hardware used in homes, hospitals and factories.

The IoT security market is forecast to hit $80.3bn by 2031, and Finite State’s expanding overseas customer base points to a problem without borders: manufacturers need to know precisely what software their products contain, whether it is exploitable and how to respond.

AI-equipped attackers can now find a flaw faster than most manufacturers can figure out which of their products contain it. Governments are rightly advancing regulations to protect the public good, leaving security teams to prove that risks they identify are understood and addressed.
